title: Meridian Wellness
text:
The logbook came under the door at 07:00 on a Tuesday, same as always. This one had an addendum on the last page in <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity>'s handwriting — tighter than <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-6067-735a-8326-4aff028cb856">Rafters</entity>'s, looser than <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>'s, the slant of a kid writing fast.

ADDENDUM (D.): TOOK A SIDE JOB. NOT A CREW JOB. PERSONAL. PENDANT THING. PAYS Φ2/DAY. WELLNESS STUDY. ASKED BOOST. BOOST SAID ASK PIXEL. PIXEL SAID FINE. EVERYBODY ON IT. FOLLOW-UP: RAFTERS STILL OWES ME A DUMPLING.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it twice with his tea. "Wellness study" sat wrong. In this city, wellness meant one of two things. Either someone was selling your gait, or someone was testing a drug and wanted twelve-year-olds to test it on. Both showed up under nicer names on the same kind of invoice.

He pulled out his personal unit and photographed the page — <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity>'s handwriting, the date, the slant of it. The image came out clean. He sent it to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> without caption.

The reply came before he'd finished the cup. Three seconds — the time it took her to pull the image larger, rotate it, read it all the way through, because she read all the way through before she spoke. Then: "How many kids?"

He commed in.

"<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity> plus whoever she recruited. She's calling it a wellness study. Φ2 a day, per child."

<entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> while she moved through the projection. He could hear it opening on her end, data being called up.

"Φ2 a day is a real wage." She knew every wage in West Town; she said it the way you'd read a price back to a shopkeeper who'd rounded up. "That's not a study budget. That's a recruiting budget. Get me one of the pendants, <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity>, and give me an hour."

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity> was eleven, narrow through the shoulders, waiting on the rest of her body to catch up. The pendant rode on a cord at her throat — a flat disc of matte resin the size of a coat button. Her logbook entry on it read: PENDANT ISSUED BY WOMAN (TAN COAT? DIFFERENT TAN COAT). MUST WEAR DURING WAKING HOURS. MUST NOT REMOVE. FOLLOW-UP: IT GETS WARM SOMETIMES. NOT BAD WARM. JUST WARM.

"Different tan coat," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"There are multiple tan coats in this city." <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> was on the alley crate, arms folded, taking the news quietly. Quiet, from <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>, meant angry. "Where's it run, <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity>? You didn't log the address."

"Building on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-c53d-7304-b953-a44879ea410e">Damen</entity>. Third floor. Lady takes your name, gives you the pendant, pays you. No medical stuff. Just wear it."

"Take it off," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> said. "Right now. Cord over your head, hand it here."

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity>'s hand went to the disc and stayed there, curled around it. "Can't. She said waking hours. She said—" She stepped back, shoulder finding the brick. "She wrote my name down, <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>. She knows my name. If it comes back off the book—"

"It doesn't come back on anybody. Give it to me."

"You don't know that." Her voice climbed and cracked. "You weren't there. She said don't remove it and I'm not gonna—" She twisted away when <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> reached for the cord, ducked under the arm, and put the crate between herself and both of them, both hands clamped over the pendant now like it was the only warm thing in the alley. "I logged it. I did the log. That's the rule, right? I did the rule."

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> didn't uncross her arms. She looked at the girl with her hands full of a stranger's leash, and the leash winning, and said nothing, because there was nothing to say that <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity> was ready to hear — and the disc, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> noticed, had begun to glow faintly warm through the gaps in the kid's fingers.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity> dug out a pamphlet — good stock, not <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s grade but a real print run: <entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-1beb-71dd-9071-1877cab7d04d">MERIDIAN</entity> WELLNESS INITIATIVE, COMMUNITY SENSORY SURVEY. A logo <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't know. A shell he'd have bet resolved to a shell. He took it upstairs and slid it under <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s door without knocking.

She had it open in eleven minutes, not the hour — music running while she worked, so her hands went fast and her mouth stayed shut.

The resin case lay split along its seam in two clean halves. On the magnification plate sat a disc of optical mesh no bigger than a thumbnail.

"Tracking node," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. "Passive mesh, crowd-sourced topology. Seed these at density — one every forty feet — and they triangulate anything that crosses them. The warmth <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity> felt is the uplink. Every four hours each node pings home what it logged." She set the magnifier down with the flat attention she gave a patient's chart. "It's not a wellness study. It's surveillance infrastructure, and somebody hired children to be the infrastructure. At forty-foot spacing you'd want three hundred nodes to cover West Town." She met his eyes. "<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity> has worn it eight days. The first week of everyone's movement already shipped. That's gone. That's not a problem — it's a cost. We count it and move on."

The way she said it put the loss somewhere it could be paid instead of argued over. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> liked that about her.

"Get them all out?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> asked.

"Pull eleven pendants at once and enrollment craters and the buyer knows we found it. Then they re-seed through a vendor we've never met, and we're blind." She picked up the live node, still warm. "The collection point doesn't know what it's collecting. It just aggregates packets and ships a map." She turned the disc between two fingers. "So we don't pull the pendants. We make the map wrong."

The entity's posting arrived at 11:40, on the walk back with the breakfast she'd demanded — dumplings, not cart noodles, from the place she'd named and he'd already guessed.

CONTRACT — STANDING SCOPE UPDATE.
CLIENT: [SHELL — RESOLVES TO SHELL — RESOLVES TO NOTHING].
CLIENT NOTES THE MERIDIAN INITIATIVE IS A FUNDED PROGRAM IN ACTIVE COLLECTION.
CLIENT NOTES ITS PAYROLL STRUCTURE AND IS DISTURBED.
CLIENT'S HIRES ARE ADULTS, OR CREW WITH AN ADULT SPONSOR, PAID STANDARD RATE, ITEMIZED, ON TIME.
CLIENT NOTES: THAT IS HOW YOU PUT SOMEONE ON PAYROLL.
CLIENT'S OPINION OF THE ALTERNATIVE IS FILED UNDER: FORMAL INDIGNATION.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT CAN NAME THE RELAY'S MODEL AND FIRMWARE. CLIENT CANNOT TOUCH IT — THE BUILDING IS OFF-NETWORK BY DESIGN, WHICH THE BUILDER WAS RIGHT TO DO. THIS ONE IS THE ENGINEER'S.
ADDENDUM: MODEL AND FIRMWARE BELOW. FEE: DO NOT BILL.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stopped in front of the noodle cart and read it twice. The cart man gave him the look that meant an errand had turned into a religious experience. He forwarded the firmware string to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>.

It bounced. RECIPIENT UNREACHABLE. Not a lag, not a timeout — a clean severance, the kind you got when someone threw a physical switch. He tried again, thumbed the send with the dumplings sweating grease through the bag onto his wrist, and got the same red kickback — <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s handle was dark, had gone dark sometime in the last hour without a word, and the one channel that could carry this string was the one channel refusing to open. He stood there working it: resend, reroute through the dead-drop board, strip the string and retype it by hand into a raw message in case the forward itself was the thing getting flagged. The board timed out. The raw message hung on SENDING and didn't move.

He pulled up a diagnostic on the phone, thumb smearing the screen. The city's mesh was live — he could see the other nodes, see the throughput to the street relay, green across all channels. But his outbound traffic to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s address wasn't reaching the gateway. It flatlined at the perimeter. Not dropped. Flatlined. Like someone had cut the line between his machine and everything else and left the lights on to pretend it was still there. Somewhere between the cart and here the network had decided he was talking to no one, and the firmware — seventeen kilobytes the entity couldn't deliver itself, the piece it had handed him precisely because he had hands — was sitting inert on a phone that couldn't hand it to the only person who needed it.

The part that stuck with him — he'd understand it fully at the relay — was that the entity couldn't do this one. The building was air-gapped on purpose, isolated mesh, no external relay, and whatever the entity was, it lived in the wires, and there were no wires here. It could route contracts and move pieces on a board it read from five dimensions off. It could not reach into the street and set seventeen kilobytes into a pocket. This was hands and feet and a kid on a stairwell.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> climbed to 2E with the dumplings cooling against his ribs and the firmware string dead in his pocket like a thing that had already failed before he'd ever held it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s door was open. She was sitting on the floor in front of her rig, earbuds in, not looking up — which meant she'd heard him on the stairs and decided the answer to his arrival was silence. The music was loud enough he could hear the individual tracks bleeding: drums underneath, something that might have been strings, the kind of careful architecture that meant she'd been building it for hours, waiting for the work to tell her what to do next.

He set the dumplings on the magnification plate. Beside it, the pendant lay in two halves, dissected — the coil pulled out and laid over a strip of actual paper, the kind that didn't ping or route or get flagged by anything living in the wires. She'd printed the firmware string onto it in a hand small enough to need the plate.

She killed the music. Pulled the earbuds. Turned to face him and held the look long enough that he understood: she'd been unreachable on purpose.

"The building's air-gapped," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"Since 2218. Original spec. No wireless, no hardline out, no Substrate relay — nothing that can carry a signal past the walls." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s hands were steady. Her voice was the one she used when she was explaining why something couldn't be fixed. "Whoever built it wanted it sealed. Which means whoever's running the surveillance network has to hand-carry everything in and out. Physical media. Dead drops. Runners."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't sit. "The entity can't reach it."

"No."

"And the firmware—"

"Is the only thing that cracks the relay's watchdog. Yeah. I read the posting." She picked up a dumpling, bit into the skin, chewed without tasting it. "So the entity hands it to you because you have hands, and you hand it to someone who can walk into a building that won't let machines through. Which is a beautiful problem if you're the entity. Elegant. Completely unsolvable for everyone else."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt the E.L.F. stir in his stack — a low harmonic that meant the implant was reading elevated cortisol and trying to compensate. He breathed through it. "How many runners does it take?"

"One. Someone the building already expects, quiet enough that the staff doesn't log a thing." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> set the dumpling down untouched. "So one runner. Which means <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity>."

"No."

"Yes." She turned back to the rig, pulled up the building schematic on the secondary display — Meridian Wellness Initiative, four stories, sealed envelope. "<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity> already wears one of their pendants and turns in a reading at that desk every day. Nobody else in this operation can walk through that door without being looked at."

"There are other runners—"

"Not in network. Not trusted. Not available in the next eight hours before the collection point's next aggregation cycle." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s fingers moved across the keyboard, pulling the front desk up on the schematic. "And you're not sending a stranger into that building with the only piece of firmware that matters. You know you're not."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> understood the architecture of what she was doing — laying it out in order, not asking permission but stating the topology the way a machine would state it. No argument. No appeal. Just the fact that there was only one shape that fit the hole, and they both knew what shape it was.

"I talked to <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity> before you came up," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. "Told her what it was. Told her what the risk was. Told her the alternative is letting them map three hundred kids for whatever comes next." She looked at him. "She said yes. She wrote it in her log. She's ready."

The words landed exactly where she meant them to — not as reassurance but as evidence. Ready wasn't the same as safe. Ready wasn't the same as willing. Ready meant she'd looked at the math and accepted it.

"She's eleven."

"She's eleven and she's better at this than anyone else we have, and the job doesn't care how old she is — it only cares whether she can do it." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s voice didn't soften. It didn't harden either. It stayed exactly where it was, which was the worst thing about it. "After, we count what it costs and we move on. That's the rule. That's how you keep people breathing."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt the thing she wasn't saying — the thing that lived in the space between *she's ready* and *you're going to send her anyway* — and it moved through him like a blade finding the seam in armor. She was right. He was going to send her. The alternative wasn't protection; it was exposure. Pull out now and Meridian re-seeds through a vendor they've never met, and three hundred kids stay tagged, and the map keeps collecting, and nobody knows it's collecting until it's too late.

"If she gets caught—"

"She won't. She's on their log as a participant. She stands where it says she stands." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> pulled up the next image: the relay itself, a box no bigger than a shoebox, three access ports, one of them labeled FIRMWARE CORE. "The coil rides under her real pendant. It takes the desk's handshake when the fob runs — the reader's dumb by design, it reads what's there and doesn't ask how old the hand holding it is. Six seconds. Then she leaves."

She tapped the paper strip on the plate. "That's why it's printed and not carried on anything that thinks. Nothing goes past those walls that runs on a battery. The string loads off skin contact when the desk pings the coil, and if the desk finds it before the load completes, it stops being firmware and starts being evidence."

She wasn't wrong. The math was clean. The margins were thin but real.

"And if we don't time it right."

"Then she walks out early, and the building logs a breach, and Meridian knows someone found the relay, and they re-seed the network through a channel we've never met, and we're back to blind." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s hands went still. "But that doesn't happen because <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity> is good at this, and you're going to brief her like she's a professional, because she is one now."

The words landed the way they were meant to — not as permission but as fact. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt the E.L.F. settle, the cortisol dropping as the implant recognized there was no threat to model, only a decision that had already been made by the topology of the situation itself. By the geometry. By the fact that <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity> was already inside and had already written it down.

He set the firmware stick on the magnification plate next to the cold dumplings.

"When," he said.

"Tomorrow. Eighteen-forty, when she turns in her reading. She'll be exactly where the log says she is." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> picked up the stick, turned it over once in her palm like she was weighing it. "I'll walk her through it twice. You give her the operational context — what she's carrying, what it does, why the building matters. Not the fear. Not the cost. Just the shape of the work."

"And after."

"After, she comes home. We count it. We move on." She looked at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, and her eyes held something he recognized from the night she'd wept on his wrists — the thing that happened when you chose to spend someone else's safety because the alternative was worse. "She is one now," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said quietly. "And you're going to treat her like it."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> understood then that the word *she* was <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s way of naming what <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity> had become the moment she'd written it in her logbook: not a kid who'd been given a choice, but a person who'd made one. Not borrowed. Not borrowed time. Just: time. Her own time, her own choice, her own log entry, her own name on the line.

The pendant would warm in her hands for six seconds. The building would never know she'd been there. The three hundred kids would stay invisible, and <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity> would come home, and they would count the cost, and they would move on.

That was the rule.

He went downstairs to find her.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity> took the brief the way she took the dumplings: like something she hadn't expected to be handed and meant to deserve.

"You go up at eighteen-forty to turn in today's pendant reading, which is a real thing you really do," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "You stand where the log says you stand. When she runs her fob — she does it at the desk, you've watched her — your bag is on the desk too. The coil does the rest. Six seconds. Then you leave. You walk out before nineteen hundred no matter what. If anything's wrong, you leave faster and we eat the loss."

"What's the coil look like?"

"A pendant," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, handing it over. "Like yours. Wear it under the real one. If anybody asks, you found it, you thought it was a spare."

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity> hung it under the live one and looked, for a second, like a kid wearing two of something. "Logbook?"

"Logbook," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

It nearly went wrong at 18:51. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> listened to it over the open channel from the basement junction box, in a low dim light, unable to do anything but listen.

The lady ran her fob at the desk. The coil caught the handshake — <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s screen bloomed green, KEY CAPTURED — and in the same second the lady said, easy and friendly, "You've got two cords on, hon." The channel went very quiet. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hand was already on the basement stairs.

"Found it on the ramp," <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity> said, upstairs, in the bored flat voice of a kid who'd decided bored was the safest thing to be. "Thought it was a spare. Does it count for the Φ2 if I wear two?"

A pause. Four full seconds, by <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s count.

The lady laughed. "No, hon. One pendant, one wage." A rustle — the spare turned over in her fingers, then handed back. "Run along."

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity> ran along. She came down the back stairs at a walk, because <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had told her to walk, and the walk cost her more than running would have, and she did it anyway.

She handed <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> the coil at the basement door. It was warm from her skin, no bigger than a thumbnail, still pressed to the shape of the pendant it had ridden against her sternum. Her hand was shaking. Her chin was up.

"She almost—" he started.

"You handled it," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Better than I would have. Go home. You're done."

"Does it count for—"

"It counts for logbook. Go."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had the key. Then <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had a fight.

The watchdog gave her ninety seconds a cycle. Her first swap-and-resign took ninety-four. The relay locked. She held her breath. It ran its own self-heal timer — thirty seconds of nothing, the longest thirty seconds of the night. A relay that stayed locked would have been the buyer's tip, and the whole loss for nothing. Then it came back clean, logging the lock as a power blip. She had one more try before a second lock would stop reading as weather.

She made the second one in eighty-one seconds, cutting her own re-sign routine in half and trusting the cut.

At 20:14 the first forged packet went out. Eleven nodes, worn by eleven kids living their ordinary evenings across West Town, all faithfully reporting the position of a noodle cart on its slow devoted circle of <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-c53d-7304-b953-a44879ea410e">Damen</entity> and Erie and the alley by <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity>.

"Packet accepted," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, from the junction box. He could hear her hands stop shaking through the change in her voice. "Forgery's cycling. The buyer's going to open a map of three hundred people who all decided to orbit a noodle vendor at walking pace." A breath. "Data this uniform reads as a hardware fault, not a result. <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-1757-74fd-8eb3-7e497fc642ab">Five</entity>, six days, they write off the sensor batch and pull funding. The kids keep wearing pendants that now log a lie."

"Cost?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> asked, because there was always one, and she always knew it.
